1.pericope_label: O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself

schools.summary: Place the psalm before interpreting it: Delitzsch groups it with Psalms 92 and 93 by their shared anadiplosis and reports the Septuagint's assignment of it to the fourth day of the week, while Ellicott works on the Hebrew of the opening line, which is far more concise than the English and sets the tone of emphatic repetition that runs through the poem.

Fix who is being asked and what is being asked for: Calvin identifies the persecutors as domestic rather than Gentile and reads the doubled vocative as the faithful reminding God of an office that is his, and Gill insists that vengeance belongs to God alone, magistrates exercising it only as his viceregents.

Clarke notes the absence of any Hebrew or Chaldee title and the manuscripts that join the psalm to the one before, reads it against the Babylonian captivity, and warns that the English word vengeance carries a sense of angry passion foreign to the retributive justice the text asserts.

Read the verse as a petition that is also a verdict: Henry lodges it with the supreme judge, whose throne is the last resort of oppressed innocency, and adds that such prayers are prophecies; Spurgeon guards the petitioner's motive, allowing the prayer only as sympathy with right, and hears in shew thyself the promise that the bare sight of God will end the oppression.

Augustine begins from the scandal that makes the psalm necessary: men murmur at God's long-suffering when the wicked prosper, and weak minds, thinking they live well in vain, either copy the wickedness they see or refrain from wicked deeds out of fear of penalty while not refraining from wicked thoughts.

debates.question: What occasion does the psalm belong to?

positions.summary: The Babylonian captivity: there is no Hebrew or Chaldee title, three of Kennicott's manuscripts join the psalm to the one before, and the proud are the oppressors of that empire.

A liturgical setting rather than a historical one: the psalm belongs with Psalms 92 and 93 by its anadiplosis, and the Septuagint assigns it to the fourth day of the week, a tradition the Talmud preserves.
Domestic persecution rather than foreign: the foes are intestine, and such oppression is more afflictive than the open violence of the Gentile nations.

debates.question: Is it proper to pray for vengeance?

positions.summary: Yes, but only as sympathy with right and pity for those wrongfully made to suffer; a man could hardly appeal to God out of private revenge.
Yes, because the thing prayed for is retributive justice; the English word vengeance misleads by implying angry passion.
Yes, because it is asked of the only one to whom it belongs, and never claimed by the one praying; magistrates avenge only as viceregents.

outliers.summary: Records the story from the tractate Erachin that the Levites were singing this psalm, and were cut off in the middle of it, when the Chaldeans broke into the temple.
Tells his hearers that the psalm's mysteries are shut up not in order to be denied but to be opened to those who knock with piety and sincere heartfelt love.

themes: O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself.

2.pericope_label: Lift up thyself, thou judge of the earth: render a reward to the proud... The Lord knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity

schools.summary: Work from the Hebrew words: Delitzsch explains the verb of verse 4 as speech driven by strong inward impulse and flowing forth in abundance and derives the second verb from a root meaning to tower aloft, while Ellicott supplies the divine name Jah at verse 7, records the parallels to that verse's atheism in Seneca, the Homeric hymn to Demeter and Tennyson, and reads the instruction of the nations as anticipating Paul on the divine education of the heathen.

Gill reads the oppressors as the antichristian power, hearing in the hard things the mouth that speaks blasphemies and in the crushing of God's people the wearing out of the saints of the most High, and takes the atheism of verse 7 as a flattery of impunity that God's omniscience will answer.

Clarke keeps the Babylonian setting, identifying the proud as the Babylonians and the saying of verse 7 as either infidelity or the insult of men who took Jehovah for a merely provincial god; on verses 10 and 11 he presses the versions, finding no shall he not know in them and running the clause forward instead. Wesley glosses the difficult words plainly, and closes the section by turning the omniscience on the reader.

Spurgeon reads the section rhetorically: God is asked both to ascend the judgment-seat and to raise himself as a man does who means to strike, and the psalmist's answer to the scoffers uses their own verb back at them, since men who have done with God have fallen below the ox that knows its owner.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered boast themselves in verse 4 mean?

positions.summary: It derives from the Arabian title Emir, so that the evil-doers bear themselves as commanders, making themselves out persons of distinction or lording it over God's people.
Not from Emir: the Hebrew cognate means the top of a tree, so the primary sense is to tower aloft, and the verb means to carry one's self high, to strut.

debates.question: Who are the oppressors of verses 5 and 6?

positions.summary: The Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, who carried fire and sword everywhere and spared neither age, sex, nor condition.
The persecutors of the church, working by anathemas, confiscations and cruel edicts.
Domestic rather than foreign oppressors: the naming of the friendless stranger as a victim points to tyranny from within.

debates.question: How should the end of verse 10 and verse 11 be construed?

positions.summary: The words shall he not know are supplied by the translators and stand in neither the original nor the versions; the clause should run into verse 11 — Jehovah, who teacheth man knowledge, knoweth the devices of man, that they are vanity.
The literal sense of verse 11 is for they are breath, referring not to the thoughts but to man collectively, though the Greek stands as the English does and Paul quotes it so.
Take the received sense straightforwardly: God knows all things, and in particular the thoughts, much more the practices.

outliers.summary: Observes that the psalmist deliberately asks not whether he who planted the ear has an ear but whether he shall not hear, so as to prevent our humanising God, and cites Jerome's saying that God is all eye because he sees all and all foot because he is everywhere.
Turns the verse on the learned unbeliever of his own day, arguing that we ought to pity the scientific infidel rather than be humbled in his presence.

themes: Lift up thyself, thou judge of the earth: render a reward to the proud.
Lord, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked triumph?
How long shall they utter and speak hard things? and all the workers of iniquity boast themselves?
They break in pieces thy people, O Lord, and afflict thine heritage.
They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless.
Yet they say, The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it.
Understand, ye brutish among the people: and ye fools, when will ye be wise?
He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?
He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct? he that teacheth man knowledge, shall not he know?
The Lord knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity.

12.pericope_label: Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O Lord, and teachest him out of thy law... Who will rise up for me against the evildoers?

schools.summary: Ellicott renders verse 15 as a statement that judgment shall turn to righteousness with all the upright following after it, noting that the idiom of going after is the ordinary one for adherence to a cause and specially to Jehovah, and preferring to Luther's paraphrase the older question whether the Lord of all the earth shall not do right; Delitzsch reads the strophe as praise of the Lord as the sufferer's sole and trusty help.

Gill draws the comfort from the source of the chastening — not a cruel one, nor a magistrate, nor a master, but a father — and so from what it proves; he grants the intervals of respite God gives his churches in every age but looks past them to a final rest, and takes verse 15 of God's government and his justice, long apparently parted, coming openly together.

Clarke renders the verb whom thou instructest and is precise about what God supplies — reason, then revelation set before it, then the Spirit to dispel the darkness, but no new faculty, only the old one cleared and invigorated; on verse 15 he proposes a change in the pointing that yields a different sense altogether. Wesley keeps to the plain reading of the promise.

Henry reads the turn as looking above the instruments of trouble to the hand of God, which gives it another name and another colour, and insists that the good is done not by the chastening but by the teaching that expounds it; Spurgeon hears the harp tuned to softer melodies, adds that affliction without the word is a furnace with no flux, and turns the cry for a champion on his own century.

positions.summary: That judgment shall turn to righteousness, ending the apparent contradiction, with all the upright in heart adhering to it as men adhere to a cause.
That God's government and his justice, which had seemed parted while the righteous suffered and the wicked prospered, will be seen to come together.

Read shall sit rather than shall return, by moving one letter: until the just one shall sit in judgment, and after him all the upright in heart — the just one being Cyrus, who carries that epithet in Isaiah.

debates.question: What is the rest promised in verse 13?

positions.summary: The end of the days of adversity, which are numbered: he that sends the trouble will send the rest, and teaches his people by their troubles precisely to prepare them for deliverance.
Inward rest: the man God instructs has quiet in his own soul under the chastening.
The intervals of respite God gives his churches in every age, and beyond them a final rest after the slaying and rising of the witnesses.

outliers.summary: Reads the cry for a champion as a verdict on his own century — error invading on every side, a false charity enfeebling the valiant men of Israel — and says that one John Knox would be worth a mint at the hour.

themes: Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O Lord, and teachest him out of thy law;
That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be digged for the wicked.
For the Lord will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.
But judgment shall return unto righteousness: and all the upright in heart shall follow it.
Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? or who will stand up for me against the workers of iniquity?

17.pericope_label: Unless the Lord had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence... he shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the Lord our God shall cut them off

schools.summary: Ellicott anchors the words: silence is the silence of the grave, the root behind the multitude of thoughts means dividing and so anxious, the verb of comfort means literally to stroke and so to soothe, and the throne of iniquity is an apt name for an oppressive government whose framing of mischief by a law is the making of legislation into a means of wrong; Delitzsch settles the grammar of the verb rendered have fellowship, refusing the passive some read into it.

Gill reads the extremity of verse 17 as the church's at the slaying of the witnesses and hears in the throne of iniquity the pretension of antichrist to be God's partner, closing with the tradition that the Levites recited the last verse at the fall of both temples.

Clarke works image by image — the propping of anything that is falling, the natural fortifications among the rocks of Judea — applies the gathering of verse 21 to the trial of Christ, keeps the Babylonian reading of the psalm to its end, and quotes the old Psalter's rendering of the last verse. Wesley identifies the comforts of verse 19 as God's promises and the memory of his care.

Spurgeon presses the argument at each turn: nothing but mercy can hold up a slipping foot, since no appeal lies to any fancied merit; thrones that plead a right divine while legalising robbery are a fraud upon mankind, and righteousness is the one element a lasting order requires; and faith, reading the present in the light of the future, ends the song without a trembling note.

debates.question: What is the silence of verse 17?

positions.summary: The silence of the grave, as elsewhere in the Psalter; the versions render it more bluntly still, the Vulgate in hell and the Greek in the invisible world.
Either death, where no testimony can be borne, or a speechless shame in which the psalmist would have had no word against his enemies.
The church's extremity at the slaying of the witnesses, from which the Spirit of life raises her.

debates.question: What are the multiplied thoughts of verse 19?

positions.summary: Perplexed and distressing thoughts, the word being used of the thick entwined branches of a tree — of God's majesty, of one's own sin as perhaps unpardonable, of the law by which one finds oneself carnal.
Anxious thoughts, from a root meaning to divide, the mind cast now this way and now that.
Griefs, following the Greek and Latin, the consolations answering to the multitude of the sorrows.

outliers.summary: Breaks into the first person on verse 18, saying the verse has been true ten thousand times and especially to the writer of the comment.

themes: Unless the Lord had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence.
When I said, My foot slippeth; thy mercy, O Lord, held me up.
In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
They gather themselves together against the soul of the righteous, and condemn the innocent blood.
But the Lord is my defence; and my God is the rock of my refuge.
And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the Lord our God shall cut them off.
